newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Serbs face pressure over Bosnia local elections.
newsitem.headline: Serbs face pressure over Bosnia local elections.

text.p: Bosnia's Serbs on Friday faced new pressure to lift a threat to hold their own local elections without international supervision, Western officials said.

The body charged with overseeing elections under the December 1995 Dayton peace accord for Bosnia, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), was making intensive efforts to bring the Bosnian Serbs back into line.

Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic this week told OSCE mission head Robert Frowick that the Serbs planned to hold their own local elections under their own rules, with the OSCE merely acting as an observer.

"The newly constituted National Assembly of the Republic of Srpska (the Bosnian Serb entity) will call for local elections in the RS and create the rules for them, which it has the right to do under the Dayton agreement," Plavsic said in a letter she handed to Frowick.

The OSCE has called municipal elections in Bosnia for November 23 and 24. It supervised elections for a three-man rotating presidency and other parliamentary assemblies on September 14, with nationalist parties emerging as winners.
The OSCE said in response to Plavsic's letter that the hardline Bosnian Serb leader had signed a document extending the OSCE's mandate to cover the municipal elections.

"We are coordinating our efforts with the leaders of Republika Srpska to keep that mandate viable and to keep up the momentum for the municipal elections in November," OSCE spokesman David Foley said.
Frowick was scheduled to meet Plavsic later on Friday in the Bosnian Serb town of Banja Luka to discuss the local elections.

The OSCE chief was expected to tell Plavsic that the Bosnian Serbs risked losing their share of international reconstruction aid if they continued to reject OSCE supervision, sources in the international community said.
If the Bosnian Serbs did however agree to come back into line on the municipal polls, their officials would be offered a greater role in running the elections.
The Serbs had argued that since they had a legally elected parliament of their own following the September 14 poll, they had the right to run their own municipal elections.
"They have a big point there," one international official said.

At the same time, they have pointed to irregularities in the September 14 election -- an improbably high turnout in Bosnia and allegations of Moslem ballot stuffing -- as evidence that they would be better off without the OSCE.
The international community has been stepping up the economic pressure on the Bosnian Serbs to cooperate with the new Bosnian presidency, parliament and other joint institutions.

The five-nation "contact group" on Thursday warned the Serbs they risked losing international funds designed to help rebuilding their country, a message also brought home by a visiting British Foreign Office minister, Sir Nicholas Bonsor, in talks with Serb leaders in Bosnia.
Bonsor met Serb presidency member Momcilo Krajisnik on Thursday and was expected to remind Plavsic on Friday of the economic consequences of non-cooperation.
